content: The studies conducted by Alvarez-Uria et al. (2012), Thomas et al. (2011), and Kilewo et al. (2009) excluded children who tested positive for HIV at six weeks of age. Similarly, Jamieson et al. (2012) excluded cases of HIV transmission at two weeks, while Marazzi et al. (2009) excluded cases at four weeks. Jamieson et al. (2012), Thomas et al. (2011), and Kilewo et al. (2009) did not directly report transmission rates. However, these rates were calculated based on the number of children at risk as provided in their respective studies. Marazzi et al. (2009) did not provide confidence intervals for their data, which were subsequently calculated using a specific formula. Jamieson et al. (2012) provided estimates of postnatal HIV transmission at 28 weeks (seven months) and 12 months in three study arms, including groups where mothers were on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and infants received nevirapine prophylaxis or placebo. The postnatal transmission rates at 28 weeks and 12 months of age, with 95% confidence intervals, were reported for breastfed children in three different study arms by Jamieson et al. (2012). Two studies reported the number of infections at six months but did not specify the number of children at risk. Thakwalakwa et al. (2014) documented three infections before six months among 280 children born, but no information was provided on loss to follow-up or deaths. Giuliano et al. (2013) reported four transmissions before six months among 288 children, but the number of children at risk of transmission at six months was unclear. Among seven studies reporting transmission rates at 12 months, five provided overall HIV transmission rates (including peripartum transmission), while two reported postnatal transmission rates. Coovadia et al. (2012) excluded transmissions before six weeks of age, and Jamieson et al. (2012) excluded those before two weeks. Ngoma et al. was the only study to report an estimated overall transmission rate (including peripartum) at 18 months, with lifelong ART provided to all mothers. Transmission rates at 12 months of age, with 95% confidence intervals, were reported for breastfed children whose mothers were on ART. Peltier et al. (2009) provided an overall transmission rate at nine months, including perinatal transmission, with no transmission after breastfeeding cessation. Among 227 children at risk, four infections were reported, with only one occurring after six weeks. Only 15 mothers were reported to have mixed-fed their children, and none of these children were infected. No study provided transmission rates stratified by infant feeding modality (exclusive breastfeeding or mixed feeding). All studies recommended exclusive breastfeeding for six months, and it was assumed that mothers adhered to this recommendation. Alvarez-Uria et al. (2012) noted that one infected child was mixed-fed but did not provide transmission rates by feeding modality. Additional information was requested from each study regarding how feeding type was assessed and supported, but only two studies responded. The quality of the studies included in this analysis was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. All studies were rated as very low quality due to observational designs, indirectness, and substantial heterogeneity in transmission rate estimates. Inconsistencies in the data and lack of detailed feeding information further contributed to the downgrading of study quality. The studies varied in their endpoints for peripartum transmission. Coovadia et al. (2012), Alvarez-Uria et al. (2012), Thomas et al. (2011), and Kilewo et al. (2009) excluded children who tested positive at six weeks, while Jamieson et al. (2012) excluded those at two weeks, and Marazzi et al. (2009) excluded those at four weeks. Transmission rates were calculated based on the number of children at risk provided in the studies. Confidence intervals were calculated for studies that did not provide them. In Coovadia et al. (2012), infants were randomized to receive extended nevirapine prophylaxis or placebo until six months or breastfeeding cessation. Jamieson et al. (2012) compared HIV-free survival in children whose mothers were on ART, infants on nevirapine, and a control group, with further stratification based on maternal nutritional supplementation. Alvarez-Uria et al. (2012) compared transmission rates between breastfed and formula-fed infants, with all mothers on ART and newborns receiving prophylaxis. Thomas et al. (2011) reported that all mothers were on ART, and all infants received a single dose of nevirapine within 72 hours of birth. Ngoma et al. (2015) was the only study with high adherence to ART, where all mothers received lifelong ART, and feeding practices were well-evaluated. However, the study did not stratify outcomes by feeding type, and the number of mixed-fed infants was not provided.
